description_en: Ajayamerukoṭa is located approximately 4 km northwest of Amargaḍhī, the headquarters of Dadeldhura district. The majority of the monuments in this area are situated on the right bank of the Chaurī Gāḍ river, which is a tributary of the Mahakali (or Sharda) river that forms the western border between India and Nepal. Other contemporary constructions can be found in the vicinity, such asDDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112,DDL0113andDDL0120.The Ajayamerukoṭa area is known for its rich collection of monuments, most of which were erected during the 14th and 15th centuries. According to D. P. Ojha, Ajayamerukoṭa served as a local capital for the Khasiya kings from Jumla, specifically the Khaśa Malla emperors of the 12th-14th century (Ojha 1989, p. 54). From the mid-14th century onwards, Ajayamerukoṭa gained greater significance as the capital of the Doti kingdom, particularly during the reign of King Niraya Pāla (approximately 1362-1383 CE). It was around this time that Doti emerged as an independent entity separate from the Khaśa Malla empire. This political and economic growth is evident in the numerous monuments constructed during the latter half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.The monument in question faces east and is preceded by a pavilion (bhaiṭak, DDL0131) at its entrance. Adjacent to the pavilion is another identical śikhara temple (DDL0132). All three structures are situated on a shared stone platform.The monument has undergone reconstruction by Nepal's Department of Archaeology, as indicated by the visible inventory numbers found throughout the structure. Consequently, some elements may have been displaced, lost, or stolen, and missing blocks have been replaced with newly carved ones.No divine images are carved on the temple, but a elaborately decoratedjalaharī(water spout) with a makara head is placed at the base of the northern wall. This feature, used for pouring liquids like milk and water overśivaliṅgas, suggests that the temple likely housed aśivaliṅgain its now empty sanctum.This style of architecture, with a central pavilion (maṇḍapa,baiṭhak) flanked by twośikharas, is uncommon in far western Nepal but can be found at the Bhurtī Temple Complex in Dailekh district (DLK0015). However, there are structural differences between the Bhurtī and Ajayamerukoṭa monuments. In Bhurtī, the pavilion was deliberately integrated into the temple design, while in Ajayamerukoṭa, the pavilion appears as an independent structure. This suggests that the architects in Bhurtī drew inspiration from pre-existing models, such as the Ajayamerukoṭa monuments, which themselves were likely influenced by temples in Uttarakhand.The oppositeśikhara(DDL0132) contains an inscription dated to 1373 CE (ŚS 1295) (Sharma 201, p. 303). This suggests that this monument was most likely constructed during the reign of King Niraya Pāla, around the same time as the other structures in Ajayamerukoṭa.
monument_assessment: Good (very few light surface damages, renovated or repaired), Restored, Rebuilt
